title: Sleep and Athletic Performance: The Effects of Sleep Loss on Exercise Performance, and Physiological and Cognitive Responses to Exercise
authors: Fullagar HH, Skorski S, Duffield R, Hammes D, Coutts AJ, Meyer T
population: Athletes and exercising adults (review of sleep restriction and deprivation studies)
findings: Most previous research reports that exercise performance is negatively affected after sleep loss, but conflicting findings leave the extent and mechanisms uncertain; some maximal physical efforts and gross motor performances can be maintained.
The few studies in athletes report a reduction in sport-specific performance after sleep loss.

Reduced sleep quality and quantity could produce an autonomic nervous system imbalance simulating symptoms of overtraining syndrome, and increased pro-inflammatory cytokines could promote immune dysfunction.
Studies of sleep loss and cognitive function report slower and less accurate cognitive performance.
The authors call the evidence equivocal and say further research is required.
limitations: Narrative review of heterogeneous, mostly laboratory sleep-loss studies; no quantitative thresholds; mixed populations.
implications: Sleep loss can confound HRV/resting HR flags (autonomic imbalance), so interpret a low HRV day together with logged sleep before attributing it to training.
Evidence for a performance cost of modest sleep loss is equivocal, so sleep should raise a caution, not trigger automatic load cuts.
Supports warning copy on cognitive/coordination risk after a very short night.
